tracks.title: The file that knows too much
tracks.text: Lesson 09 point 4 — privacy. A sub-lesson, under the VFS… the disk. The last lesson left you with a sharp deal — the workspace IS the artifact, so handing someone the file hands them the project. [curious] And the instant you hear that, the worry arrives. Then sharing the file shares my agent's memory… my telemetry… my signing key? The fix isn't a checklist, and it isn't a redaction step you have to remember. It's one module that every exit consults — so the boundary can't drift between them. Sharing exposes the work… never the session that produced it. That's the whole lesson, in one line. The rest is how it holds.

tracks.title: The file that knows too much
tracks.text: First — the file that knows too much. The parent lesson ended on a promise that doubles as a threat. An agent's working directory — its notes, its drafts, its long-term memory, its decision logs — lives in the same disk as the deliverable. Hand someone the file… and you've handed them the project. Wonderful — until you read it the other way. The file that carries your finished report also carries every wrong turn the agent took getting there. Every page it read. Every key it signs with. [sighs] And this is not hypothetical. The module that fixes it says so, in its own first lines. The default exists to prevent the exact class of leak this project already hit — task tracker data, pushed to GitHub. Someone ran a bulk commit, the issue tracker rode along… and a public repo got a tour of the backlog. The lesson was cheap, because nothing secret was in those tickets. [curious] Next time it might be. So the stakes are concrete. If egress is all-or-nothing, the whole the-workspace-is-the-artifact pitch collapses — because no sane person ships a file that also ships their agent's brain.

tracks.title: The boundary
tracks.text: The boundary. The definition. A single boundary module — one source of truth for what is public and what is private — that every egress path consults before anything leaves… so the line can't drift between them. Its rule, stated once in the code — sharing exposes the work, never the session that produced it. It is exactly seventy lines you can read in a sitting. And that smallness is the design. There is no privacy SYSTEM with settings and surfaces. There is one list, in one place, that three different exits all ask the same question. [excited] Define the answer once, where you can audit it, and no exit can quietly disagree with another. The agent never has to remember the boundary… because the boundary is automatic — appended, stripped, and recorded by the engine, not by anyone's discipline.

tracks.title: Three doors, one bouncer
tracks.text: Three doors… one bouncer. There are exactly three ways data leaves a workbook. First… a git commit — the work syncs to a repo and, on push, to a host like GitHub. Second… a bundle ship — the workbook packed into a file and sent. Third… a library pack — exported to share, or to archive. Each of those used to be a place where someone could forget. Three exits would mean three chances to leak… and three lists that drift apart until one is wrong. So picture a funnel. Three arrows come in from the left — git, bundle, library — and they all converge on a single decision node before anything reaches the world. The node asks one question — is this private? Whatever it calls public continues out the right… as the work. Whatever it calls private drops into a grey box, and never moves — memory, scratch, telemetry, the signing key. [curious] One node, asked three times, is the entire guarantee. There is no fourth door that skipped the question.

tracks.title: What stays home, exactly
tracks.text: What stays home — exactly. A boundary you can't enumerate is a boundary you can't trust… so here is the real list, plainly. First, the underscore sidecars. Steps-dot-jsonl — per-tool telemetry, one line for every tool call the agent made, dead ends included. Ledger-dot-json — that same steps file, hash-chained and signed. Status, trace, and a telemetry database — pipeline state and raw working notes from live runs. Next, the directories. Scratch — the agent's thinking-out-loud. Dot-workbooks — the Ed25519 signing key, the tenant's identity… and that one never ships, full stop. Dot-beads — the issue tracker, the exact thing that leaked once. And dot-claude — operator config. Then the two private volumes — memory and tmp — long-term memory and scratch, everything except the workspace. [curious] And here's the cleverest line. Any basename that starts with an underscore and ends in jsonl, json, or db… is private. Automatically. So the day some new feature writes underscore-dreams-dot-jsonl, it is already private — with nobody editing a list. The convention does the remembering. And the module renders all of that into a gitignore file — scratch, dot-workbooks, dot-beads, dot-claude, memory, tmp, and the underscore-star globs — appended to every repo from the same single source.

tracks.title: One boundary, both forms
tracks.text: A depth rung — skippable. One boundary… both forms. Private data exists in two physical shapes, and a sloppy design would protect one and forget the other. Form one — tree files. The underscore sidecars and the dot-directories, sitting as actual files when a workbook is unpacked. Form two — VFS volumes. Memory and tmp, living as rows inside the SQLite disk, never unpacked at all. Same data… two skins. So picture a little two-column table. On the left, the volume form, inside the database. On the right, the file form, when it's unpacked to a tree. Volume memory lines up with directory memory-slash. Volume tmp with directory tmp-slash. And volume workspace — the only one that ships — lines up with a public workspace directory. [curious] The verdict of that table is one sentence. If the SQLite disk is ever unpacked into a real tree, the same volumes git already treats as private in the file form are ignored there too. One boundary… both forms. There is no clever path where data that's private as a volume becomes public the moment it lands as a file.

tracks.title: Strip, then VACUUM
tracks.text: A depth rung — skippable. Strip… then vacuum. On the bundle door, the whole privacy mechanism is two SQL statements, run against a copy of the workbook's own disk. Read them aloud. Statement one — delete from vfs where volume not in workspace. Statement two — vacuum. The first is obvious. Keep workspace, drop the rest. The second is the one people forget — and forgetting it would be a quiet disaster. A SQLite delete doesn't shred bytes. It marks pages free… and the deleted rows sit recoverable in the file's slack space until something overwrites them. [curious] Ship that file, and a curious recipient can carve your agent's memory out of the free pages. Vacuum rebuilds the file from scratch — so the deleted rows are gone, not merely unlinked. Absence… made real. Now picture the sequence. The ship step hands the disk to the stripper. The stripper deletes every volume that isn't workspace, then vacuums so nothing is carvable, and hands back a disk with only the public region. Finally, the ship step writes the receipt into the manifest — which volumes shipped, and a flat private-included, false. The recipient never has to take your word for what's inside. One honest caveat lives right here. The stripper ends in a rescue that, if the strip itself crashes on malformed input, returns the original bytes — it fails open. In practice the input is the engine's own well-formed disk… but the rescue exists, and we'd rather you know.

tracks.title: Why add dash A is safe
tracks.text: A depth rung — skippable. Why is git add dash A safe? The git door earns its safety with a single habit. On every repo init… AND before every commit… the engine appends any missing private lines to the repo's gitignore. It's idempotent — only the missing lines get added, existing content preserved — so the ignore file converges to the full list and stays there. And that one habit is what makes bulk staging safe. A git add dash A is the natural thing an agent reaches for… and ordinarily it's a footgun. It sweeps in everything — including the dot-workbooks signing key. [curious] Here it can't. The auto-gitignore has already excluded session and secret data before the add runs. Picture that gitignore — scratch, dot-workbooks, dot-beads, dot-claude on one line… memory and tmp on the next… the underscore globs after… and the punchline as a comment — a bulk add physically cannot stage the signing key. The key is a host-side secret whose private half must never enter version control — the ledger's whole attribution model rests on it staying home. And the agent never has to think about any of that. It just commits. Discipline you have to maintain is discipline that eventually fails. Discipline the engine enforces on every commit… doesn't.

tracks.title: Your gitignore is the boundary
tracks.text: Your gitignore IS the boundary. Here's the part that turns this from architecture into something you actually drive. The library door runs a second filter after the built-in defaults — it honors the repo's OWN gitignore… using git's own matcher, check-ignore, not a reimplementation. Exact git semantics. And the consequence is the most useful sentence on this page. To mark something don't-share… you mark it exactly the way you already mark don't-track — a line in gitignore. [excited] No bespoke privacy API to learn. No manifest to hand-edit. The instinct every developer already has — drop a path into gitignore — IS the share boundary. So picture the library share as a double filter, left to right. The full set of parts enters. The first node strips the engine's always-private defaults. The second node then strips anything YOUR gitignore names. And only what survives both filters ships. The first node protects you from mistakes. The second node is the one you control — it expresses your intent. And the share path respects both… without you learning a new tool.

tracks.title: Saying yes on purpose
tracks.text: Saying yes… on purpose. Privacy-by-default would be useless if you could never deliberately include the session — for a handoff, or a backup of your own work. So opt-in exists, and it's always the same explicit shape — include-private, true. Always loud, always on purpose. The library pack gives that decision a legible name — a purpose, not a raw flag. There are two. First… share — the default. It ships the work only, session stripped — for anyone you send it to. Second… archive. It ships everything, session included — for YOU, a backup of your own work. [curious] And the verdict is simple. A backup of your own work that forgot your session would be a bad backup. So archive keeps everything — a re-download of your own snapshot still has your agent's memory and logs intact. Share strips, because the person you're sending it to wants the report… not your run history. Same verb… one explicit word of difference. And whichever one you chose, the manifest records it — so a recipient can read it and see whether the session is inside, before they open anything. One thing survives the strip in every case — provenance. Even on a default share, the file is signed with the tenant's identity. The signature ships… the session log doesn't. Proof travels. The session doesn't.

tracks.title: Where the boundary ends
tracks.text: Where the boundary ends — the honest part. Five things this is not. First — the CLI can't opt in yet. The pack command always ships the stripped form. The opt-in is real, but for now it's an engine option, not a command-line flag. That's future work. Second — the strip fails open. As we said, if the stripper crashes on malformed input, it returns the original bytes rather than failing closed. The input is normally the engine's own disk… so it's a narrow window — but it's a real one, and we name it. Third — there's no dedicated test suite. We looked. There is no test file targeting this module specifically. The guarantee here is architectural — one choke point, three callers, seventy auditable lines — not belt-and-braces coverage. A real property and a real limit at once. Fourth — private isn't hidden from YOU. The boundary protects egress, not your own control plane. Your engine's surfaces still read the steps file to render live agent activity — by design. You can watch every move your agent makes. The point is only that none of it leaves. [curious] And fifth — opt-in is irreversible once sent. A recipient of an include-private bundle has everything, and you cannot un-send it. The manifest tells THEM what they got… it can't claw it back for you. Choose archive for yourself… not for strangers.

tracks.title: Questions people actually ask
tracks.text: Quick fire. [curious] Is memory deleted from my copy when I share? No. Egress rewrites a copy on the way out — the strip happens in a temp file, never against your live disk. Your memory and tmp are untouched. Can I see whether a bundle I received contains private data? Yes — open the manifest. It lists which volumes shipped, and carries a flat private-included, true or false. The receipt is right there. How do I make my own file private? Three ways, all things you already know. Give it an underscore prefix and a json, jsonl, or db extension. Or add a line to gitignore — the share honors it. Or write it into the memory or tmp volume. No special API. Is this encryption? No — it's absence, not ciphertext. The private data simply isn't in the shipped bytes. Encryption-that-ships is a different mechanism — that's sealed sections, and escrow. And does provenance get stripped too? No. The signature ships even when the session doesn't. [chuckles] Proof travels. The session log stays home.

tracks.title: Back up to the disk
tracks.text: So that's privacy. Not a system… a single seventy-line module, asked the same question by all three exits, so the boundary is defined exactly once — readable, auditable, and impossible to drift. Sharing exposes the work… never the session that produced it. [curious] If any of that felt unfamiliar, the way back up is short. This page is the sharing consequence of the disk — so the parent is the VFS, lesson nine, the disk a workbook carries. Read on to volumes — workspace ships, memory and tmp stay — or to sealed sections, where bytes DO ship, but as ciphertext. This one was about what leaves. Those are about what unlocks.
